name: cryptol
desc: Domain-specific language for specifying cryptographic algorithms
why: A domain-specific language for specifying cryptographic algorithms that can be checked against implementations with formal tools.

brief.what_it_is: Cryptol is an interpreter for version 3 of the Cryptol language, a domain-specific language for writing executable specifications of cryptographic algorithms. You feed it Cryptol source and interact with it through a REPL, where you can evaluate expressions and run checks. The `:check` command tests predicates against randomly generated test vectors, in the style of QuickCheck. The `:prove` command calls out to SMT solvers such as Yices, Z3, or CVC5 to prove predicates for all possible inputs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the Cryptol specification language was designed by Galois for the NSA Laboratory for Advanced Cybersecurity Research as a public standard for specifying cryptographic algorithms. It argues that a Cryptol reference specification can serve as the formal documentation for a cryptographic module.
brief.how_it_works: Cryptol specifications are fully executable, so designers can run and experiment with them as the design changes. `:check` runs predicates on random inputs, QuickCheck-style. `:prove` and `:sat` hand the question to an external SMT solver, with Z3 as the default. The README also says Galois builds tools that consume Cryptol specs and C or Java implementations, letting you verify that an implementation meets its spec, though this takes some work and is described on the SAW website rather than here.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux, and Windows are on the GitHub releases page; Windows also has .msi installers. Z3 must be on your PATH, since Cryptol uses it by default for type checking and for :sat and :prove. Homebrew installs a matching Z3 automatically, but on Linux you may need to download Z3 yourself, because distro packages can be old. Building from source needs GHC (9.6.7, 9.8.4, or 9.12.2, easiest via ghcup), GMP, and ncurses. Cryptol reads its library files from the embedded copy by default. To override them, copy the lib directory into $HOME/.cryptol or set CRYPTOLPATH.
brief.standout: Specifications are executable, so the same file can be run, randomly tested with :check, and proven with an SMT solver with :prove. It is aimed at cryptographers and implementers rather than general programmers. Galois also links it to implementation-verification tooling (SAW).
brief.status: Appears maintained. The README says Cryptol is under active development at Galois, cites copyright 2013-2024, and points to a CI solver snapshot dated snapshot-20260622. The docs site shows version 3.6.0.99 with versions 2.12.0 through 3.6.0 listed. I did not see a release date or last commit date, so this is inferred from the README.
brief.caveats: The homepage is only the reference manual's table of contents and contains no prose, so the description above comes from the GitHub README. Cryptol needs a separately installed Z3 at runtime. On some 64-bit Linux setups 32-bit Z3 binaries fail with a misleading 'no such file or directory' error, and the fix is to install 32-bit compatibility packages or use the x64 Z3 build. Building from source has several prerequisites and uses a ./cry wrapper script rather than a standard build command. Licensed under a three-clause BSD license. The README notes that Version 1 users should read the Version2Changes document, so older Cryptol material may not match.
quotes: Unlike current specification mechanisms, Cryptol is fully executable, allowing designers to experiment with their programs incrementally as their designs evolve.
A Cryptol reference specification can serve as the formal documentation for a cryptographic module.
The interpreter includes a `:check` command, which tests predicates written in Cryptol against randomly-generated test vectors (in the style of QuickCheck).
